name: Rūta Binkytė
affiliation: German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence (DFKI)
intro: I work on bias and safety in AI. I’m especially interested in how bias and unsafe behaviour emerge when AI agents interact with one another or with people.
background: I use behavioural experiments and interpretability methods to study bias and safety in AI, from the way agents influence one another’s decisions to how people and AI share credit for their work.
news: From 7 to 19 December 2026, I’ll visit CSIRO in Australia. We’ll study how to identify what people and AI systems each contribute when they create something together.
I’ll teach at Durham University’s summer school in July 2027.
I’m now Deputy Lead of DFKI’s Efficient and Explainable AI (E&E) group. Simon Ostermann leads the group within the Multilinguality and Language Technology department.
I’ll serve as a programme chair for the Sixth European Conference on Algorithmic Fairness (ECAF 2027) in Vilnius, 25–27 August 2027.
What does alignment training reward when oversight is imperfect? Our new paper examines conditional compliance.
My lecture on bias and safety in AI is now available from the Probabilistic AI School.
Our ICML position paper uses causality to explain why trustworthy AI objectives can conflict.
Our study of hidden bias in LLM-assisted peer reviews was accepted to ACL Findings.
Coefficient Giving is supporting our project on deception in multi-agent systems. I’m leading the project as principal investigator.
I presented my framework for evaluating interactional fairness in multi-agent systems at AIES.

projects.name: AI Deception Dynamics
projects.question: Exploring deception in behavior and internal representations.
projects.description: My collaborators and I study how language-model agents respond to misleading reports from their peers. We also test what a probe of a model’s internal activity can tell us about whether its answer is deceptive.

projects.name: DFG International Collaboration
projects.question: When a person and an AI create something together, how can we tell what each contributed?
projects.description: With CSIRO’s Data61 and Macquarie University, I’m exploring how to attribute contributions in human–AI co-creation. In scientific writing, for example, a record of drafts and model interactions can help trace who proposed an idea and who developed it.

projects.name: MARSS
projects.question: How can students recognise when an online post is trying to manipulate their emotions?
projects.description: MARSS is developing a school learning platform that examines text and images together. Its feedback helps students discuss how digital media can shape their judgement and decide when to question a source.

projects.name: COMBO (Compliance Bot)
projects.question: How can AI help people work out which EU rules apply to their organisation?
projects.description: COMBO is developing a multilingual assistant that uses AI agents to help organisations navigate EU regulation. The project includes use cases for small and medium-sized enterprises working across languages.

projects.name: PriSyn
projects.question: Can synthetic health data preserve what researchers need to learn?
projects.description: At CISPA, I worked with colleagues and project partners on synthetic health data. PriSyn examines how to preserve the statistical properties needed for medical research while protecting the privacy of the people whose data were used.
